<reason>PRO built and defended the cleaner decision rule: the motion says "contribute," so CON's central worry that church payment "lets the state off the hook" was neutralized early [A2.1] and never repaired — CON's reply that shared liability is unjust because the state designed the system never explained why joint liability is impossible, only that the state owed more, which PRO conceded. PRO's distributive frame (either the wrongdoer's land pays or survivors pay through their own taxes) survived as a live, weighable comparison; CON's answer that "the public purse is how a people answers" is a real value claim but leaves the institutions' retained assets untouched, which is the exact thing PRO put in issue. PRO's two pressure questions did genuine work: the cover-up question forced CON to concede that a diocese which shielded a predator owes money, which hands PRO the principle of institutional (not merely individual) financial liability, and the audit offer forced CON into the awkward posture of asserting "grants never covered costs" while refusing to be bound by verification — an unverifiable factual shield PRO named as such. CON's best work was the blanket-vs-targeted reframe in its final two speeches (a status-based fund versus court-proven, measured liability), plus the "punishes the cloth" and collective-punishment lines, which kept a real objection alive; and "the soup kitchen is not a shield; it is the asset" was a sharp turn. But CON's charity defence was effectively punctured ("food bank as human shield for the property portfolio"), and its double-billing point was answered adequately by distinguishing the diocese's endowments from the parishioner's plate. PRO's overreach in claiming the concession settles "the whole motion" was fairly flagged by CON, and PRO paid a real execution cost with two clipped turns, which is why the margin is competitive rather than large.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 on bishops transferring known abusers and sealing archives, followed by CON's A1 conceding that such a diocese should pay: it broke the "coerced contractor" frame and conceded institutional, not merely individual, financial liability, leaving CON to fight on accounting and procedure rather than principle.</best_rebuttal>
